questions.question: Describe what a making plan contains, how it is linked to the drawings and the specifications, and the difference between a prototype and a final product.
questions.expected_answer: A making plan lists every step in order, who does it, the material and tool needed and the time allowed, with parts made before assembly and no gluing before the dry fit is right; materials are listed with quantities and spare, tools are listed for signing out, and time is spread over the making weeks with a margin before evaluation. It is written against the isometric drawing and development, which are the maker's instructions, and against the specifications, so steps that affect a specification are marked for a check such as a stack test after the rib is fitted or a leak test after gluing. A prototype is made at the scale and in the materials that answer the team's questions, full-size in real material for a container or 1:10 in card for a drain guard, and the plan states what it will and will not test; it is not the final product.

questions.question: State the safety rules for craft knives, for hot tools and adhesives, and for the Technology room during making.
questions.expected_answer: Knives: hold like a pen with the blade low, cut along a steel rule drawing towards the body and never towards the hand on the rule, keep that hand's fingers on top of the rule, use a fresh blade and several light passes, cap or close the knife when set down, never pass it open, pass scissors handles first, cut only on a mat and dispose of blades in the sharps tin. Hot tools and adhesives: use the hot wire and glue gun only at their station with cables clear of walkways, never touch to test heat, rest the glue gun on its stand, cool hot glue on skin under water rather than wiping, cut foam with the hot wire only in a ventilated room, use solvent glues and sprays with windows open and away from heat, and default to PVA and glue sticks. Room: bags under desks and walkways clear, one person at the hot station, hair tied and sleeves rolled, eye protection when cutting wire, foam or wood or when anything may snap, full clean-up, every injury reported, and ask before using an unfamiliar tool.

questions.question: Explain marking out, the difference between scoring and cutting, how a joining method is chosen with the forces in mind, and what the making record must contain.
questions.expected_answer: Marking out transfers the development using the drawing's full-size dimensions with a sharp pencil and steel rule from a straight reference edge, checked twice, with set-square right angles and fold lines marked differently from cut lines. Cutting severs the material in light passes along the rule or in short free-hand strokes for curves, with slots cut from the corners inward; scoring is a shallow cut or firm blunt press along a fold line on the outside of the fold so the board bends cleanly without cracking. Joining is chosen for material and force: PVA tabs clamped for board, hot glue for quick strong but bulky joints, slots and tabs where parts must separate, staples or wire for mesh, pre-drilled screws for timber; a glued tab in shear is made long and wide, a bending corner gets a gusset, and a joint under pull-apart load is mechanical rather than glued. The record holds a photograph at each main step, notes of problems and fixes, and every change from the drawing, which the evaluation needs.
